ANYTHINGELSE: Of course. Thank you for asking. It means a lot to feel heard. While the memory is still complex, sharing these details feels important. On the good side, the moments of genuine human connection made all the difference. The nurse who held my hand and talked me through my anxiety right before the C-section, the lactation consultant who celebrated with me over the tiniest milestone, and my partner's unwavering support—these weren't just clinical procedures; they were acts of kindness that made me feel seen and empowered during a time I felt very vulnerable. On the other hand, the transition home was the hardest part that no one truly prepared me for. The "bad" wasn't just one thing, but a series of gaps—like the stark contrast between the constant monitoring in the hospital and the sudden isolation at home. The paperwork said to "avoid lifting," but no one practically explained how to care for a newborn and myself while doing so. I also wish there had been more proactive, nuanced conversations about mental health; being handed a pamphlet on postpartum depression isn't the same as having a provider look you in the eye, normalize the struggle, and outline a clear plan for support before you even leave the hospital. Ultimately, my biggest takeaway is that the medical system excels at the technical, life-saving aspects of birth, but the continuity of care—especially the emotional and practical support for the mother's journey *after* the baby is born—is where the real healing happens, and where there
